title: Deleting a Gene Only Where Cre Acts

scenes.tts: A whole-body knockout can kill the embryo, and it cannot say which tissue needed the gene. So you want a gene gone only in chosen cells, and maybe only at a chosen time. In 1994, Gu and colleagues deleted a piece of D N A polymerase beta in T cells only. The mice were viable, although the matching germline mutation is lethal.
scenes.visual: Mouse outline with every cell dark and a skull cross: whole-body knockout; a which-tissue question mark; then six cells where only the T cells lose the gene and the mouse lives.

scenes.tts: Cre is an enzyme from a bacterial virus. It cuts D N A at a thirty four base pair site called lox P. A floxed gene has a piece flanked by two lox P sites. It works normally until Cre acts. When two sites point the same way, Cre cuts out the D N A between them.
scenes.visual: A DNA line with a gene and a segment between two same-way loxP triangles; the gene works; Cre chip arrives, the segment loops out and is lost, the gene is broken.
scenes.caption: Cre is an enzyme from a bacterial virus. It cuts DNA at a 34-base-pair site called loxP. A floxed gene has a piece flanked by two loxP sites. It works normally until Cre acts. When two sites point the same way, Cre cuts out the DNA between them.
scenes.narration: Cre is an enzyme from a bacterial virus. It cuts DNA at a 34-base-pair site called loxP. A floxed gene has a piece flanked by two loxP sites. It works normally until Cre acts. When two sites point the same way, Cre cuts out the DNA between them.

scenes.tts: Cross a floxed mouse to a mouse that makes Cre from a promoter active in one cell type. Only those cells lose the gene. This is a conditional knockout. A second design puts a stop between lox P sites in front of a reporter gene. Cre cuts the stop out, and the reporter is read in that cell and all its descendants. A glowing cell shows that Cre acted.
scenes.visual: Two mice cross; offspring tissue of cells, only the Cre-making type deletes the floxed gene. Then a lox-stop-lox reporter strip: Cre removes the stop, the cell glows and passes the glow to its daughter cells.

scenes.tts: For timing, fuse Cre to a modified estrogen receptor. It stays out of the nucleus until tamoxifen is given. Flip, from yeast, cuts at its own F R T sites and does not recognize lox P. In flies, a yeast activator called GAL four, made in chosen cells, switches on a target gene with GAL four binding sites.
scenes.visual: A cell with CreER parked in the cytoplasm; a tamoxifen chip arrives; CreER enters the nucleus and cuts. A timeline of before and after tamoxifen. Two small strips for Flp-FRT and GAL4.
scenes.caption: For timing, fuse Cre to a modified estrogen receptor. It stays out of the nucleus until tamoxifen is given. Flp, from yeast, cuts at its own FRT sites and does not recognize loxP. In flies, a yeast activator called GAL4, made in chosen cells, switches on a target gene with GAL4 binding sites.

scenes.tts: A real result: Luo and colleagues, 2020. Floxed C L S T N three mice were crossed with a Cre line. Offspring should inherit only intact floxed alleles. When the mother carried Cre, 73 of 83 offspring had a knockout allele. When the father carried Cre, none of 114 did. Look only at offspring without Cre. From Cre mothers, 29 of 34 had one deleted copy. A deleted allele in an animal with no Cre cannot be Cre acting in that animal. It points to the germline.
scenes.visual: Two crosses side by side, mother carries Cre and father carries Cre; rows of offspring boxes colour-coded by genotype f/f, f/-; counts appear; the Cre-negative subset is boxed and 29/34 versus 54/54 shown; germline arrow.

scenes.tts: First, a reporter is not a deletion. A glowing cell may still carry the gene. The control: measure the target protein or D N A in reporter-positive cells in the same animals. Second, germline recombination was reported in over half of 64 commonly used nervous system Cre lines. Genotype every animal, and check animals without Cre.
scenes.visual: Left: a glowing cell with a floxed gene still intact, a measure-the-protein probe; right: a breeding pair, Cre-negative pup carrying a deleted allele, genotype checklist.

scenes.tts: In 2007, Guy, Bird and colleagues silenced the gene M E C P two with a removable lox stop cassette, then restored it with tamoxifen-activated Cre. Advanced symptoms reversed in young and mature adult mice. In 2012, Fuenfschilling, Nave and colleagues deleted Cox ten in oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells. Conditional deletion was needed to remove respiration only in glial cells.
scenes.visual: Glia diagram with respiration switched off in one cell type; then a gene-silenced mouse, tamoxifen, gene restored.
scenes.caption: In 2007, Guy, Bird and colleagues silenced the gene Mecp2 with a removable lox-stop cassette, then restored it with tamoxifen-activated Cre. Advanced symptoms reversed in young and mature adult mice. In 2012, Fünfschilling, Nave and colleagues deleted Cox10 in oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells. Conditional deletion was needed to remove respiration only in glial cells.

scenes.tts: In 2016, Orefice, Ginty and colleagues deleted M E C P two in peripheral somatosensory neurons and caused tactile dysfunction. Restoring M E C P two only in these neurons rescued tactile sensitivity, but not lethality. Keep this rule. A reporter shows where Cre acted, not that your gene is gone.
scenes.visual: Peripheral touch neuron in the skin and a brain; deletion in the touch neuron; rescue bar for touch yes, lethality no; closing rule on a reporter cell beside an intact gene.
